newsitem.title: USA: Fed study ties funds rate volatility to reserves.
newsitem.headline: Fed study ties funds rate volatility to reserves.

text.p: The federal funds rate could become significantly more volatile if banks' required reserves continue to decline, a Federal Reserve study said.
The study, by Fed board economists James Clouse and Douglas Elmendorf, speculated that the increased volatility would probably have little economic effect, but cautioned that was not certain.

Banks recently have been able to reduce the reserves they are required to hold at the Fed to cover deposits through the use of so-called "retail sweep programs", which shift money from reservable deposit accounts to non-reservable ones.
In early 1997, banks' required reserves stood at about $12 billion, the study said. The banks had to set aside another $7 billion or so to meet clearing balance requirements.

If total required operating reserves fell to $10 billion, the daily volatility of the fed funds rate would roughly double, the study said. "(That) would make volatility on an average day about as high as the volatility currently experienced on (settlement day)," it added.

The study said the increased volatility would complicate banks' efforts to manage their reserves. It might also have other adverse effects on financial markets, although the authors of the Fed paper doubted that.
"We suspect that increased funds-rate volatility would have fairly small effects beyond the reserves market itself, but this outcome is by no means certain," the study said.
The paper is the work of the authors and does not necessarily reflect the views of the Fed Board.
